claims.claim: Specific phobias involve intense fear out of proportion to actual danger; this plate applies that framework to fear of fire.
Anticipating a feared object or situation can cause excessive worry; encountering it can cause immediate intense anxiety.
People may actively avoid feared objects and situations or endure them with intense anxiety.
Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea.
Avoidance can restrict activities; exposure-based CBT helps people engage in activities and situations they have avoided.
CBT teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting; exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias.
Relaxation exercises may accompany exposure therapy; breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms.
Seek a primary care provider when symptoms affect life; a provider can refer to a qualified mental health professional.
Open flames are dangerous if candles tip over or are too close to combustible objects; ordinary fire precautions remain necessary.
Consider battery-operated flameless candles; lit candles need stable holders, at least 12 inches from anything that burns, and should be extinguished when leaving the room or before bed.
Use flashlights rather than candles during a power outage.

claims.claim: The pear-shaped gallbladder lies below the liver in the upper right abdomen and stores bile produced by the liver.
Bile passes through hepatic, cystic and common bile ducts into the duodenum; the pancreas also delivers digestive juices to the duodenum.
Eating signals the gallbladder to release stored bile into the duodenum to mix with food.
Gallstones are hard pebble-like material formed in the gallbladder; cholesterol stones are typically yellow-green and pigment stones are dark and made of bilirubin.

Stones may form when bile has too much cholesterol or bilirubin, insufficient bile salts, or the gallbladder empties incompletely or too infrequently; the reasons for bile changes are not fully understood.
Most gallstones are silent and do not cause symptoms; asymptomatic gallbladder stones usually need no treatment.
A stone obstructing a bile duct can cause bile buildup and biliary colic; attacks often stop when the stone moves and the blockage ends.
Pain can be severe and constant, in the upper right or middle abdomen, last several hours, and accompany nausea or vomiting; attacks often follow heavy meals.
Persistent blockage can lead to gallbladder inflammation, bile-duct infection, or gallstone pancreatitis; these are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes.
Risk is higher with older age, family history, obesity, rapid weight loss, and in women; risk factors do not establish an individual diagnosis.
Evaluation of suspected gallstones can include ultrasound and blood tests; similar symptoms may have other causes requiring clinical assessment.
The main treatment for symptomatic gallstones is gallbladder removal, often laparoscopic; ERCP may clear a stone in the common bile duct. Treatment depends on clinical circumstances.
After gallbladder removal, bile flows from the liver through the ducts directly into the duodenum rather than being stored in a gallbladder.

Healthy eating with fiber, regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight and avoiding rapid weight loss can help reduce gallstone risk; they do not guarantee prevention or dissolve existing stones.

Seek urgent medical care for sudden severe abdominal pain, pain lasting several hours, fever or chills, jaundice, or pain spreading to the back with vomiting; dark urine and pale stools may accompany complications.

claims.claim: A cataract is clouding of the natural lens; the normally clear lens bends incoming light to help vision.

claims.claim: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease, often starting in childhood but possible at any age; it is not contagious.
Barrier changes allow moisture to escape and expose the skin immune system to the environment; genes, immune activity and environmental factors contribute, and there is no single known cause.
Skin has a protective outer layer; a schematic intact-versus-disrupted surface comparison illustrates moisture retention versus increased water loss, not a literal hole through the whole skin.
Inflammation can trigger itch; scratching causes further skin damage and inflammation and increases bacterial infection risk.
Symptoms include intense itching, dryness, cracking, scaling and thickened skin; scratches may bleed or weep clear fluid.
Eczema appearance varies with skin tone: it can appear red, purple, grey or lighter or darker than surrounding skin; inflammation may leave color changes.
Common sites include elbow and knee bends and hands; babies often have facial eczema. Distribution varies by age and can occur elsewhere.
Symptoms fluctuate between flares and improvement; itch can disturb sleep.
Family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever is associated with increased likelihood, not proof of one cause.
Soap, detergents, fragrances, rough fabrics, heat and stress may worsen symptoms; triggers vary by person.
Diagnosis involves clinical skin examination and medical, family and trigger history; clinicians may use tests to rule out other causes.
Regular moisturizing, including immediately after bathing, helps retain water and supports the skin barrier; gentle unscented or non-soap cleansing and lukewarm water can help.
Avoid personal irritants, keep cool and keep nails short to reduce scratching damage; do not change diet unless advised by a clinician.

Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation; other topical treatments, phototherapy or systemic medicines may be considered by clinicians depending on severity, age and response, not as universal treatments.
Treatment can control symptoms but there is currently no cure; seek care for symptoms or treatments that are not helping.

Painful warm swollen skin, pus, sudden worsening or spreading, fever or feeling unwell, and new blisters or leaking/crusting can signal infection or eczema herpeticum and warrant urgent medical advice.
Emollients transferred onto clothing, bedding or dressings can make fabrics catch fire more easily; avoid smoking and naked flames.
